title: Switching & PWM
description: Why converters switch instead of burning the excess voltage, how duty cycle and PWM set the average output, and how switches are built from MOSFETs and diodes.

study.title: Why switch?
study.body: A linear regulator drops the excess voltage across a transistor that carries the full load current, so its efficiency can never exceed $V/V_g$. Stepping 100 V down to 50 V at 10 A that way burns 500 W. A **switch-mode converter** uses only elements that ideally dissipate nothing: switches that are fully on or fully off, inductors and capacitors. Real converters reach 90–98 %, so heat sinks shrink and the converter gets small and light.

study.title: The ideal switch
study.body: An ideal switch is either **on** ($v = 0$, any current) or **off** ($i = 0$, any voltage), so the power $p = vi$ it absorbs is always zero. Resistors and transistors in their linear region are kept out of the power path. Real losses come from the small on-state voltage, the finite switching speed and parasitic resistances (see the unit Switching Losses & Thermal).

study.title: Explore: duty cycle and the switch node
study.body: The switch connects the **switch node** to $V_g$ for $DT_s$ and to ground for the rest of the period, $D'T_s$. $D$ is the **duty cycle**, $D' = 1 - D$, and $T_s = 1/f_s$ is the switching period. The average of this rectangular wave is $DV_g$. Drag $D$ (here $V_g$ = 24 V).

study.title: Filtering: the buck converter
study.body: A low-pass LC filter between the switch node and the load passes the DC component $DV_g$ and strongly attenuates the switching harmonics at $f_s, 2f_s, \dots$, because its corner frequency $f_0 = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$ is far below $f_s$. The result is the **buck converter**: an ideally lossless DC–DC converter with $V = DV_g$. The $n$-th harmonic of the switch-node wave has amplitude $\frac{2V_g}{n\pi}\left|\sin(n\pi D)\right|$.

study.title: Pulse-width modulation (PWM)
study.body: A PWM modulator compares a control voltage $v_c$ with a sawtooth of peak value $V_M$ running at $f_s$. The gate signal is high while the sawtooth is below $v_c$, so $D = v_c/V_M$ (for $0 \le v_c \le V_M$). A feedback controller moves $v_c$ to keep the output at its setpoint when $V_g$ or the load changes. Drag $v_c$ ($V_M$ = 2 V).

study.title: Realising the switch: MOSFET and diode
study.body: In practice the changeover switch becomes a **MOSFET**, turned on and off by its gate, and a **diode**. When the MOSFET turns off, the inductor current must keep flowing: it drives the switch node negative until the diode conducts, so the diode switches by itself. A MOSFET conducts in either direction when on and blocks positive $v_{DS}$ when off (its body diode conducts for $v_{DS} < 0$). A diode conducts positive current and blocks negative voltage. Replacing the diode by a second MOSFET, a **synchronous rectifier**, cuts the conduction loss at low output voltages.

study.title: Averages and rms of switched waveforms
study.body: Switched currents are pulses, so their average and rms values differ a lot. A pulse of height $I$ and duty cycle $D$ has average $DI$ but rms value $\sqrt{D}\,I$, and the rms value sets the conduction loss $I_{rms}^2R$. A DC current $I$ with a triangular ripple of peak deviation $\Delta i$ (half the peak-to-peak value) has an rms value of $\sqrt{I^2 + \Delta i^2/3}$, barely above $I$ for small ripple.

steps.title: Linear regulation wastes power
steps.body: A linear regulator acts like a variable resistor in series with the load. The full load current $I$ flows through a transistor that has $V_g - V$ across it, and all that power becomes heat. Its efficiency is therefore at most $V/V_g$.

steps.prompt: A linear regulator makes {{V|V}} at {{I|A}} from a {{Vg|V}} input.

ask.prompt: How much power does the pass transistor dissipate?
ask.explanation: $P_{loss} = (V_g - V)I$ = ({{Vg}} − {{V}}) V × {{I|A}} = **{{(Vg-V)*I|W}}**, while the load only receives {{V*I|W}}.
Input and output current are the same, so $\eta = \frac{VI}{V_gI} = \frac{V}{V_g}$ = {{V}} / {{Vg}} = **{{100*V/Vg|%}}**.

steps.title: Switches, inductors and capacitors
steps.body: An ideal switch has either zero voltage (on) or zero current (off), so $p = vi = 0$ at every instant. Ideal inductors and capacitors store energy and return it without loss. A converter built only from these elements can change the voltage level at 100 % efficiency; real ones reach 90–98 %.

steps.prompt: An ideal switch dissipates no power, both when it is on and when it is off.
steps.explanation: On: $v = 0$, so $p = vi = 0$. Off: $i = 0$, so again $p = 0$. Loss only appears in real switches, through the on-state voltage drop and during the transitions when $v$ and $i$ are both non-zero.

steps.prompt: A converter delivers {{Po|W}} with an efficiency of {{eta*100}} %. How much power is lost as heat?
steps.explanation: $P_{in} = P_{out}/\eta$ = {{Po|W}} / {{eta}} = {{Po/eta|W}}, so $P_{loss} = P_{in} - P_{out} = P_{out}(1/\eta - 1)$ = **{{Po*(1/eta-1)|W}}**.

steps.prompt: You need {{V|V}} at {{I|A}} from {{Vg|V}}. How many times more heat does a linear regulator produce than a switching converter with {{eta*100}} % efficiency?
steps.explanation: Linear: $(V_g - V)I$ = {{(Vg-V)*I|W}}. Switcher: $P_{out}(1/\eta - 1)$ = {{V*I|W}} × (1/{{eta}} − 1) = {{V*I*(1/eta-1)|W}}. Ratio: {{(Vg-V)*I|W}} / {{V*I*(1/eta-1)|W}} = **{{(Vg-V)/(V*(1/eta-1))||3}}**. The heat sink of the switcher can be that much smaller.

steps.prompt: Which element would you keep **out of** the power path of an efficient converter?
options: A resistor that carries the load current
A MOSFET that is driven fully on or fully off
steps.explanation: A resistor converts $I^2R$ into heat. Inductors and capacitors only store energy, and a MOSFET that is either fully on (small $v$) or fully off (no $i$) dissipates little. The resistor is the only lossy element by nature.

steps.prompt: Match each element to how it handles power
steps.explanation: Ideal switches and reactive elements absorb no average power, which is why a switching converter can in principle reach 100 % efficiency. A linear pass transistor has voltage and current at the same time, so it dissipates $(V_g - V)I$.

steps.title: Duty cycle
steps.body: In every period $T_s = 1/f_s$ the switch connects the switch node to $V_g$ for $t_{on} = DT_s$ and to ground for $D'T_s$. With $f_s$ = 100 kHz, $T_s$ = 10 µs; $D$ = 0.3 means 3 µs at $V_g$ and 7 µs at 0 V.

steps.prompt: A converter switches at {{fs|Hz}} with a duty cycle of {{D}}. How long is the switch in position 1 (connected to $V_g$) each period?
The switch node of a {{fs|Hz}} converter sits at {{Vg|V}} for {{ton|s}} of each period and at 0 V for the rest. What is its average voltage?
steps.explanation: $D = t_{on}f_s$ = {{ton|s}} × {{fs|Hz}} = {{ton*fs||3}}. $\langle v_s\rangle = DV_g$ = {{ton*fs||3}} × {{Vg|V}} = **{{Vg*ton*fs|V}}**.

steps.title: The LC filter keeps the average
steps.body: An inductor and a capacitor form a low-pass filter whose corner frequency is far below $f_s$. They pass the DC component of $v_s$ and block the switching ripple, so the load sees $V = DV_g$, anywhere from 0 to $V_g$ depending on $D$. This is the **buck converter**.

steps.prompt: A buck converter must make {{Vo|V}} from 12 V. Which switch-node waveform is right?
steps.explanation: $D = V/V_g$ = {{Vo}} / 12 = **{{Vo/12||2}}**, so the switch node must be high for {{Vo/12*100|%}} of every period. The waveform with $D$ = {{1-Vo/12||2}} would give {{12-Vo|V}}: a common slip is to mix up the on and off times.

steps.title: The PWM modulator
steps.body: The gate signal comes from a comparator: a sawtooth with peak value $V_M$ rises once per period, and the output is high while the sawtooth is below the control voltage $v_c$. The on-time is therefore proportional to $v_c$, and the controller sets the duty cycle simply by moving $v_c$.

steps.prompt: A PWM modulator has a sawtooth peak of $V_M$ = {{VM|V}}, and the control voltage is {{vc|V}}. It drives a buck converter with $V_g$ = {{Vg|V}}.

ask.explanation: $D = v_c/V_M$ = {{vc}} / {{VM}} = {{vc/VM||3}}, so $V = DV_g$ = {{vc/VM||3}} × {{Vg|V}} = **{{Vg*vc/VM|V}}**. The modulator plus power stage behaves like an amplifier with gain $V_g/V_M$.

steps.prompt: The sawtooth of a PWM modulator has a peak of {{VM|V}}. Set the control voltage $v_c$ so that the gate signal has a duty cycle of {{Dt}}.
steps.explanation: The gate is high while the sawtooth is below $v_c$, i.e. for the fraction $v_c/V_M$ of each period. So $v_c = DV_M$ = {{Dt}} × {{VM|V}} = **{{Dt*VM|V}}**.

steps.prompt: Doubling the switching frequency of a buck converter at the same duty cycle doubles its output voltage.
steps.explanation: $V = DV_g$ does not contain $f_s$. A higher $f_s$ only makes the ripple smaller (or allows a smaller $L$ and $C$), at the price of higher switching losses.

steps.prompt: A MOSFET carries a rectangular current pulse of {{I|A}} for a fraction {{D}} of each period and nothing otherwise.

ask.explanation: $I_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{T_s}\int_0^{T_s} i^2\,dt}$ $= \sqrt{D I^2} = \sqrt{D}\,I$ = √{{D}} × {{I|A}} = **{{sqrt(D)*I|A}}**, larger than the average {{D*I|A}}.

steps.prompt: A MOSFET with $R_{DS(on)}$ = {{Ron|Ω}} conducts a {{I|A}} current pulse with duty cycle {{D}}. What is its conduction loss?
steps.explanation: $I_{rms}^2 = DI^2$, so $P = I_{rms}^2R_{DS(on)} = DI^2R_{DS(on)}$ = {{D}} × ({{I|A}})² × {{Ron|Ω}} = **{{D*I^2*Ron|W}}**. Using the average current instead ($(DI)^2R$) would underestimate it by a factor $1/D$.

steps.prompt: An inductor carries {{I|A}} DC with a triangular ripple of {{pp|A}} peak-to-peak. What is its rms current?
steps.explanation: The peak deviation is $\Delta i$ = {{pp/2|A}}. $I_{rms} = \sqrt{I^2 + \Delta i^2/3}$ = √({{I}}² + {{pp/2}}²/3) = **{{sqrt(I^2+(pp/2)^2/3)|A|4}}**, only {{100*(sqrt(1+(pp/2/I)^2/3)-1)|%|2}} above the DC value.

steps.prompt: The switch node of a converter swings between 0 and {{Vg|V}} with duty cycle {{D}}. What is the amplitude of its fundamental component at $f_s$?
steps.explanation: For a rectangular wave, harmonic $n$ has amplitude $\frac{2V_g}{n\pi}|\sin(n\pi D)|$. For $n = 1$: 2 × {{Vg}} / π × sin(π × {{D}}) = **{{2*Vg/pi*sin(pi*D)|V}}**. It is largest at $D$ = 0.5, and it is what the LC filter must suppress.

steps.prompt: The fundamental of a buck converter's switch-node voltage has an amplitude of {{V1|V}} at $f_s$ = {{fs|Hz}}. The LC filter has $f_0$ = {{f0|Hz}}; far above $f_0$ its gain is about $(f_0/f)^2$. Estimate the amplitude of the $f_s$ component at the output.
steps.explanation: $|H(f_s)| \approx (f_0/f_s)^2$ = ({{f0|Hz}} / {{fs|Hz}})² = {{(f0/fs)^2||3}}. Output: {{V1|V}} × {{(f0/fs)^2||3}} = **{{V1*(f0/fs)^2|V}}**. A second-order filter falls at 40 dB/decade, so a 100× lower $f_0$ gives 10 000× attenuation.

steps.prompt: A switch current is a rectangular pulse of height {{I|A}} with duty cycle {{D}}. What is its rms value?
steps.explanation: $I_{rms} = \sqrt{D}\,I$ = √{{D}} × {{I|A}} = **{{sqrt(D)*I|A}}**. $DI$ is the average, $I$ the peak, and $\sqrt{1-D}\,I$ would be the rms value of the complementary (diode) pulse.

steps.prompt: The graph shows the switch-node voltage of a converter switching at 100 kHz. What is its average value?
steps.explanation: Read $t_{on}$ = {{D*10e-6|s}} out of $T_s$ = 10 µs, so $D$ = {{D}}. $\langle v_s\rangle = DV_g$ = {{D}} × {{Vg|V}} = **{{Vg*D|V}}**.

steps.prompt: The rms value of a current can never be smaller than its average value.
steps.explanation: $I_{rms}^2 = \langle i^2\rangle$ $= \langle i\rangle^2 + \langle (i - \langle i\rangle)^2\rangle$, which is at least $\langle i\rangle^2$. They are only equal for pure DC. Pulsed currents in converters therefore cause more $I^2R$ loss than their average suggests.

steps.prompt: In this buck converter, tap every element that must block the full input voltage $V_g$ during part of the switching period.
steps.explanation:
- MOSFET on: the switch node is at $V_g$ and the diode is reverse biased with $V_g$ across it.
- MOSFET off: the diode conducts, the switch node is ≈ 0 and the MOSFET blocks $v_{DS} = V_g$.
The inductor sees $V_g - V$ and $-V$, the capacitor $V$. Both semiconductors need a voltage rating above $V_g$ plus margin.

steps.prompt: A buck converter is built with a MOSFET but the diode is left out. What happens at the first turn-off?
options: The inductor drives the switch node far negative ($v = L\,di/dt$) until something breaks down
The inductor current stops and the circuit simply idles
The output capacitor discharges back into the source
steps.explanation: An inductor current cannot change instantly. Without a path, $di/dt$ is huge, so $v_L = L\,di/dt$ forces the switch node very negative until the MOSFET avalanches or another part fails. The diode provides the path the current needs while the MOSFET is off.

steps.prompt: In a buck converter the inductor current is {{I|A}} (ripple negligible) and $D$ = {{D}}. The freewheeling path is either a diode with $V_F$ = {{VF|V}} or a synchronous MOSFET with $R_{DS(on)}$ = {{Ron|Ω}}.

ask.prompt: What is the diode's conduction loss?
ask.explanation: The diode carries $I$ during $D'T_s$: $P_D = V_F I D'$ = {{VF}} V × {{I|A}} × {{1-D||2}} = **{{VF*I*(1-D)|W}}**.

ask.prompt: What is the synchronous MOSFET's conduction loss?
ask.explanation: $P = I_{rms}^2R_{DS(on)} = D'I^2R_{DS(on)}$ = {{1-D||2}} × ({{I|A}})² × {{Ron|Ω}} = **{{I^2*Ron*(1-D)|W}}**, versus {{VF*I*(1-D)|W}} with the diode.

steps.prompt: A power MOSFET that is turned off can block voltage of either polarity.
steps.explanation: Its body diode conducts as soon as $v_{DS}$ goes negative, so a MOSFET only blocks positive $v_{DS}$ (and can conduct in both directions when on). Blocking both polarities needs two devices in anti-series.

steps.prompt: Match each device to its role
pairs: Switches by itself when the current reverses
Turned on and off by its gate
MOSFET used in place of a diode
steps.explanation: Active switches (MOSFET, IGBT) are controlled by a gate signal; passive switches (diodes) are commutated by the circuit voltages and currents. A synchronous rectifier is a MOSFET timed to conduct when the diode would, with a lower voltage drop.

steps.prompt: A buck converter delivers {{V|V}} at {{I|A}} with $D$ = {{D}}. The MOSFET has $R_{DS(on)}$ = {{Ron|Ω}} and the diode $V_F$ = {{VF|V}}; ignore ripple and switching losses. What is the efficiency (in %)?
steps.explanation: MOSFET: $DI^2R_{DS(on)}$ = {{D*I^2*Ron|W}}. Diode: $D'V_FI$ = {{(1-D)*VF*I|W}}. $P_{out}$ = {{V*I|W}}. $\eta$ = {{V*I|W}} / ({{V*I|W}} + {{D*I^2*Ron|W}} + {{(1-D)*VF*I|W}}) = **{{100*V*I/(V*I+D*I^2*Ron+(1-D)*VF*I)|%}}**. At low output voltages the diode drop dominates.

steps.prompt: Put the events of one switching period of a MOSFET + diode buck converter in order, starting when the gate goes high.
items: The MOSFET turns on; the switch node rises to V_g and the diode is reverse biased
The inductor current ramps up with slope (V_g − V)/L
The gate goes low and the MOSFET turns off
The inductor current forces the diode on; the switch node drops to ≈ 0
The inductor current ramps down with slope −V/L
steps.explanation: The MOSFET sets the interval $DT_s$; the diode takes over automatically for $D'T_s$ because the inductor current must continue. The inductor voltage is $V_g - V$ in the first interval and $-V$ in the second.
